sentences.text: Brontornis was an extinct genus of giant flightless birds that lived in Argentina during the Early to Middle Miocene.
Based on fossil finds, Brontornis is estimated to have reached a height of 280 cm, with the species B. burmeisteri standing about 2.80 meters tall.
The massiveness of its bones leads to weight estimates between 319 and 400 kg for the largest individuals.
The animal is known from fossils of legs, feet, some skull parts, and vertebrae found in the Santa Cruz province.
Some fossil finds show size differences of up to 33% based on the tarsometatarsus.

Brontornis is considered the fourth-heaviest bird ever found, after Aepyornis maximus, Dromornis, and Pachystruthio, though it is currently the third heaviest bird known after Aepyornis maximus and Dromornis stirtoni.
It was the dominant carnivore in Patagonia during the Miocene, capable of killing large animals like the elephant-like mammal Astrapotherium and the predator Thylacosmilus.
The genus Brontornis was described by Moreno & Mercerat in 1891, marking the first time fossils of this creature were identified by Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat.
The initial fossils consisted of a left femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, and tarsometatarsus from a single individual found in the Santa Cruz Formation of Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
Fossils described as B. platyonyx are about one-third smaller than the largest Brontornis bones.
Brontornis is related to seriemas and shares features like a hook-shaped upper beak and curved, sharp claws, indicating it was a predatory carnivore.
Researchers suggest it may have hunted by jumping on prey and knocking it down with attack force after a short chase.
Studies on the lower jaw indicate it was likely not suitable for tearing animal food.
The taxonomic position of Brontornis is controversial, with it being alternatively classified as a cariamiform, a phorusrhacid (terror bird), or an anserimorph.
Cladistic studies have suggested that Brontornis is a basal relative of geese.
A 2017 study suggested that Brontornis belongs to the sister taxon of Cariamiformes.
A 2021 study classified Brontornis as a Gastornithiform.
It has traditionally been included in the family Phorusrhacidae, or "terror birds," due to its large size and predatory lifestyle.
Brontornis lived during the Early to Middle Miocene, and the fossil range of Brontornis spans from the Early Miocene to the Middle Miocene.
The absence of the bone footbridge (Pons Supratendineus) found in Phorusrhacids is a point used to argue against Brontornis being a terror bird.
The different design of the lower jaw suggests Brontornis had a different diet than Phorusrhacids.
Recent studies have questioned whether Brontornis is a phorusrhacid, suggesting instead that it is actually an anseriform.
However, a later analysis interprets Brontornis traits as adaptations for supporting its weight while showing diagnostic thoracic vertebrae of phorusrhacids, reaffirming its membership in that group.
Some researchers believe Brontornis could have been a carrion eater due to its original placement within the "terror birds" grouping.
